common_name: Mrs. Howard Asper Camellia (Giant Rose-Pink Peony-Form Camellia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Mrs. Howard Asper is grown for its exceptionally large, heavy blooms on a compact, well-branched plant.

directions: Named by camellia breeder Howard Asper for his wife, this cultivar produces some of the largest flowers in the genus, often exceeding 6 inches across, in a rich rose-pink peony to anemone form with broad, wavy outer petals surrounding a dense center of petaloids. It has long been a favorite on the camellia show circuit for its sheer size and full form, blooming in midseason on a slower-growing, compact, well-branched evergreen shrub. Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, and mulch generously to keep roots cool and evenly moist. Disbudding side buds encourages the terminal bloom to reach its maximum size, and light pruning immediately after flowering maintains a dense habit.

common_name: Julia Drayton Camellia (Historic Deep Red Formal Double Camellia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Julia Drayton is a historic Lowcountry cultivar long associated with Magnolia Plantation near Charleston, South Carolina.

directions: One of the classic old Southern camellias, Julia Drayton bears large, deep crimson-red flowers in a formal double to loose peony form, with rows of overlapping petals that age to a slightly darker wine red. Grown for generations in Charleston-area gardens and closely tied to the historic collections at Magnolia Plantation, it blooms from midseason into late winter on a vigorous, upright, densely foliaged evergreen shrub. Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, and mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to keep the root zone cool and evenly moist. Prune only to shape and remove dead wood immediately after flowering.

common_name: General Colletti Camellia (Red and White Marbled Peony-Form Camellia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; General Colletti is a nineteenth-century European introduction long naturalized in old Southern garden collections.

directions: Dating to the mid-1800s, General Colletti produces semi-double to loose peony-form flowers in deep red irregularly marbled and streaked with white, no two blooms marked quite alike, giving plantings an old-fashioned, variable character prized by heirloom camellia collectors. It flowers in midseason on a vigorous, upright evergreen shrub that has been passed down through Southern gardens for generations. Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, and mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to maintain even soil moisture. Prune only to remove dead or crossing wood after bloom, since flower buds form on the current season's growth.

common_name: Marchioness of Exeter Camellia (Large Pale Pink Semi-Double Camellia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Marchioness of Exeter is a historic English cultivar valued for its very large, softly ruffled flowers.

directions: A historic nineteenth-century English introduction, Marchioness of Exeter bears very large, semi-double to loose peony-form flowers in a soft, pale pink with gently ruffled, waved petals that give the bloom an informal, romantic fullness. It flowers over a long midseason to late-season window on a vigorous, upright, well-foliaged evergreen shrub that has remained popular in heirloom camellia collections. Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, and mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to keep the root zone evenly moist. Prune lightly to shape immediately after flowering.

common_name: Elegans Splendor Camellia (Rose-Pink and White Marbled Anemone-Form Camellia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Elegans Splendor is a marbled sport of the classic 'Chandleri Elegans' anemone-form camellia.

directions: A sport of the old anemone-form favorite 'Chandleri Elegans', Elegans Splendor bears large rose-pink flowers irregularly marbled with white, with a mass of petaloids and stamens crowded at the center in the same anemone form that made its parent cultivar famous. It blooms in midseason on a slow-growing, spreading evergreen shrub prized in heirloom camellia collections for its variable, hand-painted-looking blooms. Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, and mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to maintain even soil moisture. Prune only lightly after flowering to preserve its naturally graceful, spreading habit.

common_name: C.M. Hovey Camellia (Historic Dark Red Rose-Form Double Camellia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; C.M. Hovey is one of the oldest named camellia cultivars still in American cultivation, dating to the mid-1800s.

directions: Introduced by the Hovey & Company nursery in the 1850s, C.M. Hovey is one of the oldest named camellia cultivars still grown in American gardens, producing rose-form double flowers in a deep, dark red with tightly imbricated petals arranged in neat concentric rows. It blooms in midseason on a slow-growing, upright evergreen shrub that has persisted in old garden collections across the South for well over a century. Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, and mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to keep the root zone cool and evenly moist. Prune only to remove dead or crossing wood after flowering.
